utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin and Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, good afternoon to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. General Talic, good afternoon to you too. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand? I see that your microphone is not on. THE ACCUSED TALIC: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am hearing you in a language I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. My name is Andrew Cayley. I appear on behalf of the Prosecutor with my learned friend Ms. Korner and our case manager Denise Gustin. Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Good afternoon to you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am attorney Milan Trbojevic. With me is lead counsel Mr. John Ackerman and our assistant Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Appearances for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Zecevic and Natasha Ivanovic-Fauveau for General Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you too. So Mr. Ackerman, regarding the -- regarding the matter you raised yesterday, I -- we have made a find-out. And rather than taking time from the sitting itself, I suggest that during the first break you contact Madam Registrar who has all the information and the sort of a workable -- not exactly solution but a workable way out to lessen the inconvenience as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're very grateful, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm here just briefly, although I will come back later if I may. About this afternoon: Regrettably, as we rather suspected, the witness is really too tired, having arrived last night and having been seen this morning by Mr. Nicholls to commence testifying today. I'm not sure how much longer there is for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were given to understand that we roughly expect about an hour and a half as a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, it's really hard to deal with the remainder of the session, not to waste time. There are some administrative matters. For example, it would help if Your Honour were able to help us about days off Your Honour mentioned for the next quarter, as it were. There's two or three small matters that I want to mention. But effectively that won't take very long. I was wondering whether we could deal with this afternoon -- so I'm given advance notice -- with one aspect, which is slightly troubling, which we haven't yet dealt with, and it's really connected with the questions Mr. Ackerman was asking yesterday. Sometime ago Mr. Ackerman wished to tender the transcript of the examination and cross-examination in a previous case of a witness unrelated to these matters, and it was rather left in abeyance. And I wonder whether we could solve that, because it is connected with a matter that I do want to raise, and that's this question of how witnesses are being questioned about handwriting. It seems to me that we will need some kind of ruling from Your Honour about the nature of this, and I wondered whether we could deal with that after this witness has finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: With regard to the transcript that I submitted as an exhibit, if I haven't already done so - I think I did, but if I haven't I withdraw it - and if I'm going to submit it again at all, it will be under Rule 92 bis in the Defence case. With regard to the issue of handwriting, you know, I don't -- I don't make those documents. I just look at them. And that has to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's why I think it might be perhaps advantageous if we could just discuss the general principle of -- of this line of cross-examination at the moment, because it's obviously something that's it's -- it's come up now -- it's the second time it has come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, it has come up the second time. I am not at all worried about the first time when it came up. I am a little bit concerned with regard to the second time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. So may I suggest, if it's a way of at least dealing with that particular issue after this witness has been completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If the Defence is prepared to -- to discuss that today. I mean, it seems that you are prepared and therefore if you want to, I would definitely give you time. But I don't know if the Defence is prepared to discuss --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not -- at the moment, when I say "prepared," Your Honour, obviously I was keeping an eye on yesterday's proceedings. And I noticed it was coming up. It's not that I was suggesting at this stage that we talk about authority. It's just the general principles. And if need be -- and there needs to be a proper legal discussion, that can be adjourned. But I'd like to just deal with the principles at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there any objection on your part? I don't think there should be any objection at this point. The way she has put it -- the way Ms. Korner has put it, I think we can live with it today and then we'll see later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I don't mind her taking time to tell Your Honours what it is she believes ought to be done with regard to that issue. I may want some time to respond to what she has to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- this is why I have pointed that out myself, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It also may be a very simple matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could well be. It could well be. Because as you know, there has -- between what happened yesterday and what happened during the testimony of the previous witness, Draganovic, there's quite -- quite a difference and quite a substantial difference, because one witness confirmed one time after another that in spite of appearances, that was his signature, while the one we had yesterday himself could not confirm it, at least in an -- unequivocal manner. And anyway, I mean, to be very frank with you, even before you -- he started giving evidence, I knew exactly what questions you would be asking him in that direction, because I -- I have two eyes like you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Well, I think, Your Honour, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's definitely worth dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm sorry. I didn't have my microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It definitely calls for a ruling in due course, also because to continue upon what I was telling you, when I went home yesterday in my mind I had to come back on this matter and make it clear to Mr. Ackerman that if the Defence or if he intends to ask for the appointment of -- nomination of a calligraphic expert, that this be done in good time, and not be postponed, and postponed, and postponed until we are then suddenly faced with it. Anyway, this is something that I wanted to come back to. But I think we can discuss it later on when we finish with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the last thing, Your Honour, is I don't know how much time that will leave. It really depends on the cross-examination -- was -- I tremble each time I mention the word, but documents. If there's any spare time, would Your Honour consider perhaps going through some -- in court through some of the -- we never actually covered anything other than the first volume of the Banja Luka documents. I knew it -- I knew it would provoke this reaction, and I think it probably provoke this is reaction from Your Honours as well. And I know -- I know that it's difficult, but it does seem to me -- the trouble is the further we move away from Banja Luka, the less likely it is that we are going to look at these documents at the convenient time. But Your Honour, I'm mentioning it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's see how much time we have left anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what will be the mood then, especially from the two Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would Your Honours -- would you consider, each of you, individually assuring Ms. Korner that you will read her exhibits. If you would do that, maybe she would get over this. Because I just don't want to sit here another two or three hours while she reads to us. It's just bizarre. All of you are capable of reading and you are professionals and you will do it; I know you will. And this just -- if she's going to do it, then I would ask leave to be excused, because I don't want to sit through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll come to that later, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the witness. And we will inform you roughly -- in good time --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To you and all those present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And we'll go through the same procedure as yesterday and the time -- the day before. Please repeat the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. And I'm sorry for keeping you waiting this time 12 minutes -- shorter than yesterday -- a shorter time than yesterday but still 12 minutes. Again, we had some problems to deal with; nothing to -- that concerns you as such. And Mr. Zecevic for General Talic will be resuming and continuing with his cross-examination of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, yesterday we broke when we were talking about the period when you were working in the water pump station in Zdena. On the first day, on the 24th of June, you told us that one evening while you were working there at that water pumping station you saw some trucks with weapons, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You saw those trucks close to the building of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The social club.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in that building of the social club there was a branch of the Territorial Defence, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. All I can confirm is that meetings were held there, and I said who was present at those meetings. I cannot claim that the institution you mentioned was housed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You noticed those trucks in the evening, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just before dusk. But visibility was quite sufficient for me to recognise and see at a hundred metres distance the trucks and the people around the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, on the first day you said that those men that you saw, that you just referred to, that you saw them from a distance of 100 metres, were mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that they were all inhabitants of three streets, Kolonija 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a part of the Zdena local commune intercepted by three streets called Kolonija 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know any of those people?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that just then I personally was able to recognise by name any one of them, because as I said on the first day, I didn't want or dare to linger there. It was just a moment when you become breathless, you see what's going on, and then you withdraw to avoid any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your observation lasted a minute or two for you to notice all this.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Would you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was saying your observation of this incident consisted of you throwing a glance in that direction, so it didn't take more than a minute or two if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite sufficient, Mr. Zecevic, for me to have a clear understanding of what was going on. If necessary on another day, my kum, Marjanovic Drago and Jovo --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Just give me -- just answer my question.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just going to say that I have corroboration from Serbs that this was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On the first day you said that those people were wearing olive-green uniforms.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me add, also camouflage. They were not all in the same kind of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was that location lit up when you noticed it?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need, because one could still see well. That part of Kolonija in those days and even today doesn't have any public lighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Islamcevic, is it not correct that around about that time there was an operation of the takeover of weapons from the Territorial Defence throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina, that this operation was ongoing?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- if I may, I could link this to what happened, because I told my director that the public utility company had purchased two semi-automatic rifles, and I said, "If those weapons are going to the warehouse of the Territorial Defence, does that mean that the next day that weapons -- those weapons will be pointed at me even though I contributed to the funds to purchase them?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm grateful for your explanations, but could you please focus on my questions. My question was: Are you aware that around that time, end of March/beginning of April, an operation was underway to take over weapons from bodies of the Territorial Defence throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of those activities in Sip, the largest company in the mines, and in other companies but not on the streets and not in such locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the weapons that you saw, were they unloaded in boxes or individually?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with certainty that it was handed from one hand to another, from one man to another. So what you observed was a group of people standing behind the truck and handing weapons to people standing behind the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you allow for the possibility that the weapons were being loaded onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to something else. During your testimony the day before yesterday you said that you were aware of a paramilitary formation known as SOS.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also said that they had some very clear insignia.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said "clear insignia"? Could you explain briefly what they were like.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very brief terms, a ribbon round their foreheads with the letters "SOS." Some had armbands also, but mostly these were ribbons round their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, are you quite sure that all the members of this paramilitary formation wore some sort of insignia?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in the municipality building of Sanski Most and moving across the bridge and in the park, I had occasion to see people that I knew belonged to that unit without wearing those ribbons during the daytime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, in your statement you said that that paramilitary organisation started to throw grenades around town in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And setting fire to Muslim houses as well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you also mentioned that grenades were thrown at shops and businesses owned by Muslims, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Were they thrown exclusively at Muslim property?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Exclusively it was Muslim property that was at risk as a result of these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the property of Croats, members of the Croat ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few, insignificantly, as compared to the Muslim property. There were some individual cases, but nothing like the number against Muslim property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that on the 14th of April, 1992 a grenade was thrown at a cafe owned by a Serb, a member of the Serb nation?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just now I can't remember, but I can claim with certainty that there were such cases as well. But again, with certainty I can claim on the basis of my own knowledge, Your Honours, that these were mutual settling of accounts between members of the Serb nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During the past two days you spoke to us about the significance of a person called Vlado Vrkes. You frequently spoke to Vlado Vrkes regarding various problems, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As many times as I have informed you during my testimony here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So very frequently; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you were able to see how many times. Five to seven times at least during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that in the second half of June 1992 - this is page 88 of the transcript of the 24th of June, line 14 - that you called representatives of the SDS, including Vrkes, to come to a meeting at Pobrijezje, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked them kindly to come. I invited them to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You asked them to come and they came. They accepted and they came.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After a couple of days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You chaired that meeting, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather say that it was a -- an assembly meeting of people lost and crying out for help to people and appealing to their humaneness to assist if they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did you chair that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that meeting the members of the Muslim ethnicity had a rally, and on that occasion you were elected as one of the representatives of the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of five.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you -- that sometime in July 1992 you asked to talk to Vrkes and that representatives and presidents of other local communes be invited to that meeting so that they may too explain in person their positions and give the reasons why they wanted to leave Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. And I explained what were the reasons and what occurred prior to that because we wanted to hear the position of all. This was prior to the first trip to Dvor Na Uni, which did not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us that you insisted on all representatives of local communes being invited because, among other things, at what point in time you were being accused of collaborating with the Serbs and you wanted everyone to state clearly their positions and demands, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was done by uninformed Muslims and Bosniaks. Those who were well informed and were aware of my mission at the time knew well that by accepting to do this, I was risking my own life and that of my family. But it was worth trying, sir. It was worth it because of human dignity, to look people in the face and tell them that they are mistaken and that I am not what they think I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, your answer to my question is yes.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context in which I answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On page 22 of yesterday's transcript you said - and I'm going read it out to you. I'll read it out to you in English since the transcript is English and then it will be interpreted to you: [In English] "It was clear to me that we were on the same wavelength and that we had the same objective, which was to save our lives, not to have our families separated, and to move onto territory which was more secure. At the end of that meeting --" and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Is what I have just read out correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It's correct that most people shared my opinion, and it's also correct to say that some of those who listened to the official authorities from Sarajevo, who kept saying "Don't leave your homes," and someone thought they had the right to make my situation and that of my families uncertain, even if that person was perhaps Mr. Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, I deliberately read out this part of your statement in the transcript that you gave on page 78, line 12 to 14, and in the testimony you gave yesterday you said that you all had the same reason and the same motives for wanting to leave; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ask me why we all had the same reasons, what preceded that. That's just the result of something that happened prior to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, yesterday you explained in detail the background of these events, the background of this. I'm just asking about this meeting and about the other representatives from local communes. Had you all agreed?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand you very well, sir. If you had been by my side, you would have reached an agreement too. That's quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion -- or rather, after that you made a certain document which was so to say a summary of what had been said at that meeting. It explained your reasons, and in essence it explained what you would say at the next meeting in Topusko; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Among other things, in that document, if I have understood you correctly - since we haven't seen the document - among other things, you said that the Serbian -- you alleged that the Serbian authorities were not in a position to secure education, medical care, pension schemes, et cetera; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the president of the municipality of Sanski Most made a very clear statement and his collaborators too -- after he said that they wouldn't be in a position to provide such security. And I want to ask -- I want to put a question to you. Did they really want to provide such security?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, isn't it true to say that at that time, the middle of 1992, the schools and the municipalities weren't working and no education institutions either?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to remind you of something. The situation was unclear for many. The president himself, Mr. Karadzic, said, "This isn't going to last for very long. Be patient. You'll work, and we Serbs will wage a war." There was some sort of logic. If that doesn't last for long, then the conditions would be created for those children to go to school, to be educated. There was some sort of logic to this idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Is it true to say that at that time the schools were not open, nor any other educational institutions?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's forget about the summer holidays. But to tell you the truth, the schools that were there, they weren't open, they weren't functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, Mr. Islamcevic --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, allow me. My son Harris Islamcevic enrolled in the first class in October. The school is called, the primary school Narodni front, the national front primary school. So yes, he did enrol in school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, isn't it true to say that in Sanski Most, at that time, you often had the electricity supply cut off?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were such cases too. For technical reasons, yes, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Given that you worked in the water -- for the water supply, you know that your water supply was made in such a way that when there was no electricity in the town, there was no water either.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you will allow me to say so, as far as the pump is concerned it would fill up a basin which had a certain amount of cubic metres. I won't go into details. And for a certain period the town could be supplied with water. Up until the time that you would accumulate sufficient water, the amount of water that had previously been accumulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The situation with regard to electricity and electricity shortages, that situation affected the entire town of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We all suffered the same fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, Mr. Islamcevic, that at that time, the middle of 1992, because of the situation, pensions weren't paid out to anyone either?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true too. But later on certain payments were made. The Serbs would receive payments, but not the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the middle of 1992. It's a very specific question, so please just refer to that period.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it also true to say that at that time because of the situation in the market there wasn't enough food and there wasn't enough medicine either?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, let me tell you something: There was enough food in Sanski Most, more than enough. I don't know where all those lorries -- or in a certain sense I do. I don't know where all these lorries went to, towards Banja Luka. What remained that -- if that had remained, there would have been enough food for the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims, or in whatever record you -- order you want to put them. But it's true to say that during that period and later on, there was a crisis, if we are talking about food.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's return to the meeting in Topusko. You told us that you went to that meeting with Mr. Vrkes, Mr. Majkic, and Eso, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Majkic Dragan, and Eso, whose surname I still don't know, and I don't know whether he survived. We went there in one car.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you also told us that you found out in Topusko that Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Anicic with the driver Vlasto was in another car.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found that out, and I saw them. I saw the lieutenant colonel. On one occasion he took half a piece of bread from me. We had direct contact. We saw each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Anicic was a pensioner?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that many JNA officers before the conflict broke out, they had been retired and they were at the disposal of the Republika Srpska and the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in your statement in 1999 given to the investigators of the Prosecution, on page 5 of that statement, the fifth paragraph and the last sentence in that paragraph, you said that Mr. Anicic didn't attend the meeting in Topusko.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, yesterday you also told us that while you were driving towards Topusko, at a certain checkpoint on the road from Prijedor to Bosanski Novi you saw a group of Chetniks with Seselj's photograph and that Seselj was a Yugoslav citizen and someone who lived in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that's not just some checkpoint, but it's a checkpoint which is as you enter the main road for Bosanski Novi. So the location is in the municipality of Prijedor. It's the exit from the municipality of Prijedor. I apologise, but I said the truth. Those people, they were people that I had seen in partisan films. They were given a name that we used. If they're not ashamed of using that name, why should I be ashamed of saying what they were, of using that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You are surely aware of the fact that Mr. Seselj was born in Bosnia and Herzegovina and that he had lived in Sarajevo and worked as an assistant at the law department in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He graduated in -- from a university in the USA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You know that he was an assistant in the law department in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know a lot about that gentleman and about his position with regard to Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Muslim people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, yesterday you went into details about your conversation with representatives of the UN, and you told us both about the official part and about your conversation which wasn't attended by Vrkes and other Serbian representatives; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at that point you said that you told UN representatives about the events in Trnovo, Hrustovo, and Vrhpolje; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And your information about those events came from third parties. It's hearsay information; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally heard information about Trnovo. Hrustovo was hearsay information from Serbian sources and from Muslim sources, very reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean Trnovo was -- you had personal information about Trnovo?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening the SOS forces with a few lorries and something that they had made armour on so that they could mount a rifle on it, they came about 30 metres from me and I could see them quite clearly. I could see who they were and what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, on that occasion you spoke about the involvement of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That information of yours was also hearsay information to say the least.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my neighbours who were members of the 3rd Battalion, inhabitants of the Podlug local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, who is in question? Who are you talking about, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can remember. I can remember Juga, Peda, Mikan Tepic, Predrag Banic, other Tepics, Kuzmanovics, Radujko, Vujkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's quite enough, sir. The 3rd Battalion was in fact a unit of the Territorial Defence; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you. I think it was part of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you what it was a part of, but I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is no, it wasn't the Territorial Defence. It was a military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the investigators for the Prosecution dated 1999, on page 7 of that statement in the second paragraph, in the Serbian version -- it's the first paragraph in the English version -- you said you had never addressed Mr. Basara; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And how should I say this to you? On the 1st of May in a cinema in Sanski Most that officer -- a former JNA officer -- I think that he was also mentioned. He had -- he was wearing two hats. It was quite clear to me who he was and what he was. I thought that it wasn't necessary for me to address him, but the result of that conversation would have been quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to this meeting in Topusko. If I have understood your testimony correctly, the testimony you gave yesterday, your main objective and your principal request with which you went to that meeting was to ensure that there were convoys -- organised convoys under the control of the UN and in a certain direction which would also make it certain that families wouldn't be separated and that those who wanted to leave would actually manage to reach that destination; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said. And please don't take that part out of context, because then it gets a different meaning. Then I seem to be the organiser of the convoy and not the Serbian authorities. And all those preconditions which led to the idea that it would be necessary to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This request of yours wasn't accepted by the representative of the UN.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And he said that he didn't have the mandate to move anyone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your first statement, the 13th of February, 1995, you said in the police station in Travnik, I think --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security service centre in Banja Luka with its headquarters in Travnik. That's what its real name was, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion you stated that the Serbian authorities had agreed that it would be possible to leave Sanski Most freely and that anyone who wanted to could go abroad. This took place on the 27th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under the conditions that they imposed. So there was no guarantee to move out. There was no guarantee that children would not be separated from their parents, because those who were military fit well, you know very well, just as I do, where they ended up. This is not a matter for discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us an anecdote on that occasion in Topusko when Vrkes and Majkic were arrested because they hadn't announced their arrival, and it was in another state and the anecdote amounted to saying that you weren't arrested but they were.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was incredible to think that two Muslims could move around Topusko without any protection, and on the other hand Serbians, high-ranking officers, not ordinary Serbians, high-ranking political representatives of a party which was in power, were where they were -- well, that was quite incredible. But they were immediately recognised, and it was no longer a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just want to clarify this. They were arrested by the Serbian polices of the SAO Krajina which at the time existed in the Republic of Croatia and that territory was under Serbian control; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want to use the word "arrest," well, it wasn't an arrest in the traditional sense. They were just -- their papers were only checked so they could determine who they were. Someone called Anicic and someone called Vrkes, that would be strange if they were arrested in SAO Krajina and imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that was really another entity. It was the Serbian Krajina, when compared with the Bosnian Krajina from where you come; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they had the same objectives, the same strategic positions, and they both knew what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's return to the convoys. Yesterday on page 33, line 7 to 11, with regard to the convoy that went -- that left at the beginning of August, when my learned colleague the Prosecutor put you a question as to whether the convoys had been organised, you said that the Serbian authorities allowed this convoy to leave and that people also left in private vehicles.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Provided that the Serbian authorities had authorised them to leave in their private vehicles, but a precondition for this was to have paid and to have paid a significant amount for this favour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, those people who went -- who left in their private cars, they joined the convoy on a voluntary basis too; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, they carried out all their duties. They signed a document saying that they were leaving voluntarily, in inverted commas, and then they joined the convoy that was leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us on page 36 of yesterday's transcript that from Mladen Lukic -- that you asked Mladen Lukic for a meeting, which was attended by representatives of the 14 local communes. They were Muslims. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was just before this convoy at the beginning of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that meeting you discussed and you tried to determine how many people would be interested in leaving, and you established that you need between 15 and 20 buses; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of people who had got this information from the field in local communes, people such as me, who had been negotiating in the name of the local communes. And we had discussed this with people who wanted to leave, because there were people who didn't want to leave too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you to make a pause for the sake of the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that when the convoy left more people came than the number of people on the list. And you told us that you read from a list and finally you said that this was your last duty, the last task you had as a negotiator with regard to that convoy in September.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just some list but a list of the inhabitants of the Pobrijezje local commune, and there weren't more people but there wasn't a sufficient number of vehicles. And at that meeting too we knew more or less what the number of people was that could be in that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the people who left in that convoy, no one so to speak made them physically leave. They didn't go from house to house and make them get on the buses. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, that was just not necessary. The house of Avdija Halilovic, Salija Salimtovic [phoen], Zikrija Hasic, Jakupovic Smajla, Rasim Jakupovic, Dimke Kamber [phoen], Fade Jakupovic [phoen] -- these houses had already been burnt and they had been mined. They had been blown up. So it was not necessary for anyone to motivate them to get on the bus. It was quite clear -- it was quite clear what had to be done and what one had to try to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, these convoys were organised in such a way on a certain day -- a certain day a certain time a certain place, was it determined. People would come then. They would get on the bus. They would form the convoy, and then they would leave. Isn't that the way it was organised?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you also told us that about three and a half thousand Muslims remained in Sanski Most, including yourself and your family.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 9th of February, 1995 when my family and I left. Not in 1992, not in the year that we are talk about right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know how many Muslims remained in Sanski Most in 1992 after the last convoy in September had left?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think that this information is not relevant at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... asked that question by Mr. Ackerman yesterday. He pointed out a particular date, which I can't remember now, but basically it was the date of his departure. And he gave a figure of 3.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours. But as he just said, it is -- it is a date in 1995. I'm asking him for the relevant time for this indictment, the end of 1992, if he can say that. It is just if he -- if he knows. If he doesn't know, he doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you know, Mr. Islamcevic, please tell us. If you don't, don't tell us. Just tell us you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't give you a precise number, but it's certainly a bit bigger than the one from 1995, because yesterday there was no discussion about the last convoy in November which was called the Capljina convoy. It was so called because that's where the present Nedeljko Rasula was born, and I think that's the safest convoy. We didn't include this figure yesterday in the number of those who left in 1992. I didn't participate in the departure and in the preparation of this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, although you didn't participate in that, do you know that people left in 1993 and 1994 too?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1993 and 1994? Yes, through the Fisher Agency. Small numbers, but you are right. There were people who left then, but through these individual agencies. Or if someone had a little money, if someone still had some money, then it was possible for individuals to move to Belgrade even.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These people, members of the Muslim ethnicity who remained at the end of 1992, including yourself, who remained in Sanski Most, you stayed on because you didn't want to leave. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not with the first wave, and I explained to the Trial Chamber why I didn't leave immediately, although I had the opportunity of joining that convoy because I already had the paperwork.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, Mr. Islamcevic, if we could summarise all of this. You have given us the reasons for which in your opinion it was not possible to live in Sanski Most, and you told us what motivated the Muslims to request to leave Sanski Most and to leave Sanski Most; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that you had asked the Serbian authorities to allow this departure and you had asked the UN to organise convoys under UN control and that finally in collaboration with the Serbian authorities you'd established how many people wanted to leave, and then you successfully organised the convoy together with the Serbian authorities; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that's a conditional answer. An please don't forget this. This is the result of something. You're talking about the consequences. But I am trying to take you back and to point out the causes of -- of these events, what led to these consequences, why the Muslim population in Sanski Most wanted to do what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Islamcevic, if I have understood you correctly, you stand by -- in spite of all of this, you stand by your position, which you repeated on several occasions -- you stand by your statement that the Muslims didn't leave Sanski Most on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't leave voluntarily, and this was caused by the physical conditions in which they were living in Sanski Most, the circumstances that they felt -- the existential circumstances they found themselves in in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please bear with me, Your Honours. There's some problem with the transcript, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, Mr. Islamcevic, you remained in Sanski Most until 1995.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Sanski Most on the 9th of February, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a statement of loyalty on the 24th in the LiveNote, page 88, line 13 actually, it was a statement accepting the citizenship of Republika Srpska, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It said Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Somebody did that intentionally. There was an indication of Republika Srpska, of Bosnia-Herzegovina, something to that effect. I saw hundreds of such statements. Unfortunately I haven't kept any one of them. I didn't know this would happen. I would be glad to give Their Honours a copy to see. And I will repeat once again that only Jews had this in the Second World War and the Muslims in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: My question was, because of the transcript, please: This statement of loyalty, was it in fact a statement on acceptance of the citizenship of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not. What do you mean Republika Srpska? It wasn't until the Dayton agreements. It was an artificial entity in those days, a product of the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, during the past two days you mentioned some local convoys as well. And on page 35, line 16 and on you mentioned the first such local convoy that went from Mahala to Velika Kladusa; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were citizens of Mahala, an area of Sanski Most, who after being expelled from Mahala found shelter in the local commune of Pobrijezje, and after a certain period of time by buses they were deported to Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I do not know who organised and took part in the organisation of this convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I am interested in is when you said at one point in the course of your testimony that the Serb army on the first day of the Bajram holiday came to Mahala, and then you mentioned Mico and there's no surname, and others head of police Majkic, and Tutic, and others. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not Mahala. It's Pobrijezje. Members of the Serb army came on the first day of Bajram to the local commune of Pobrijezje. And that is when they went from one house to another. And who was not an inhabitant of Pobrijezje had to leave, thanks to Micko, a captain of the JNA and later of the Serb army. My wife's family remained because her father was undergoing dialysis treatment and her old mother was over 82 years of age. That is when all those who did not belong to the Pobrijezje local commune were rounded up. And at the time they were mostly the inhabitants of Mahala, a local commune in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, for the needs of this transcript -- this is the third time that you're answering a question by saying no and then yes. Please, because only the no has been recorded in the LiveNote. Please tell us yes or no or I don't know or I can't say.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said no because the gentleman was using the wrong place. I said not Mahala but Pobrijezje. My answer to the rest of the question is yes. I am not trying to complicate things. I just want to make things clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely for the sake of clarity is why I made my observation. In your statement of 1995 on page 2, the last sentence, you said that the organisers and perpetrators of this persecution was the SOS?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please repeat the question. I was absent. I wasn't concentrating just then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the previous question when you corrected me and said it wasn't Mahala but Pobrijezje. And then in connection with that, I'm saying that in your statement of 1995 you said that the organisers and perpetrators of this persecution were SOS.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really have to tell you, SOS staged an attack with the help of the 6th Krajina Brigade, and I clearly saw who came to Pobrijezje and who took these people, members of the army. I did not see Njunja and his men, but possibly they were there too but I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will have to read this statement for you from 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a part that was read out to you yesterday also by Mr. Ackerman, Mr. Islamcevic. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 15th of February, 1995, page 2, the one but last sentence. "The organisers and perpetrators."

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not on that page in my version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- it's on page 2 -- Mr. Islamcevic, look at the bottom of the page. It's not that final last paragraph. It's the paragraph before. And it's the last sentence: "Organizatori i izvrsioci ovog progona," et cetera. That's the sentence that Mr. Zecevic is referring you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. The inhabitants of the upper part of Pobrijezje saw members of SOS. I life in Donja Pobrijezje, so both is true. I hadn't intended to say anything about SOS, but this realisation came later. I mentioned SOS because I had heard it. I didn't mention what I saw, the man who was at my door, in my yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, in this statement of yours you mentioned something that you personally did not know but you heard about, and you didn't mention what you personally observed.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It can be interpreted in that way. I believe it's an omission, and it wasn't intentional, Your Honours. With full responsibility, I claim that in my yard were members of the army. And at the upper end, near the bridge where the buses were, I heard from Zoric and others who were there that members of SOS were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned somebody called Boro Tadic, who was secretary of the Municipal Secretariat for National Defence, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Municipal Secretariat for National Defence is a municipal body, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So a civilian body.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who appointed Mr. Boro's secretary, Mr. Zecevic? You know that very well, how things work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, will you please answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he's a civilian, why was he wearing a military uniform? I apologise, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To clear things up, you are claiming that this municipal body, that is, the Municipal Secretariat of National Defence, is a civilian body but that this gentleman, Mr. Tadic, was wearing a military uniform; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all civilised countries, that is how it is. But the situation at the time was not normal. He belonged to that body. He signed things. I got call-up papers from him for work duty -- signed by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This means that he was a member of a civilian body, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A civilian and military body, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Talking about this subject, tell me, the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, is he not appointed by the municipality?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the system that existed before, it was quite clear who appointed him. Sir, you're on very slippery ground now. Who forced Boro Tadic to wear a uniform in Gornja Mahala and to point out which houses should be burnt? I really do apologise. I understand your position and your duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, in the course of that period of three years, did you see other civilians wearing military uniform?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Boro Savanovic; I saw Mikan Davidovic. He was in the office when the camouflage uniforms arrived. He was sitting there, and they unpacked with great satisfaction these uniforms and put them on, and they were staff members of the administration, both Savanovic and Davidovic. I don't need to enumerate others.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to another topic now. In the autumn of 1992 you continued to communicate with the municipal bodies. And when you were asked whether you wanted to go to the meeting with Vance and Owen, you said you consulted some prominent Muslim intellectuals and agreed to go, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You met Mr. Radovan Karadzic, who was at the time president of the SDS and of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you explained in detail the content of your conversation with Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Islamcevic, on that occasion did you have any reason to doubt the sincerity of what he was saying?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Slobodan. And again, yes. In spite of the statement he made in the BH parliament that one nation may disappear, I knew well who this gentleman Radovan Karadzic was, a man I could not trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is it not true that Mr. Karadzic on that occasion, during your brief conversation, asked you, among other things, why it is you wanted to leave Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to fully present the course of the conversation and the truth about the conversation we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He asked you that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes, he did ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, very briefly please, in connection with the disappearance of your father-in-law and two other persons you told us that this happened on the 27th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement that you gave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Which statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see that the witness is consulting his papers. That is why I was waiting. I will, of course, tell him what statement -- which statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at yesterday's documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that this happened on the 27th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you now that in your statement to the investigators of the Prosecution on page 6, second paragraph of the English version, paragraph 3 of the Serbian version, you said that this occurred in June, in June 1992.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The correct date is the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the night before was the attack on Pobrijezje. It's ten years now today. So this is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the course of your statement here in court you said that the driver of that ambulance told you that three soldiers took them out of the car and since then they are registered as missing.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 1995, 15th of February, 1995, on page 5, the seventh paragraph towards the end -- do you have it?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I read it. You said the following: "When they had completed the haemodialysis and on their way back to Sanski Most, in Carakovo, Prijedor municipality, a group of armed Chetniks intercepted them, took them out of the car, and executed them." That's what you stated on the 15th of February.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In February 1995 we learnt the painful truth that shortly after they left the van I went to the spot that they were executed immediately, but it took a long time for me to learn the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So it is true that a group of armed Chetniks took them and executed them.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even three men are a group. Two are not, but three are a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. My colleague is showing me that the day before yesterday you told us on page 90 of the LiveNote, line 17 -- and we're talking about the same event: [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... missing, and we haven't learned anything about them to this day."

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Translation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Shall I repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I'll repeat it. I'll repeat it myself. Mr. Islamcevic, please look at me. I'm going to repeat Mr. Zecevic's question, because I understand you had no interpretation at the time it was made. "Very well. My colleague is showing me that the day before yesterday you told us on page 90 of the LiveNote, line 17 -- and we are talk about the same event: '... missing, and we haven't learned anything about them to this day.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What date is that of the statement, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you were giving evidence here, you remember that you were telling us how you were worried when your father-in-law failed to turn up -- back from the dialysis. And at --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite sure that I said that until the end of 1992, they were registered as missing, and I didn't go on from there because we were talking about 1992. Towards the end of 1992, we didn't know. They were recorded as missing. Even in the Keraterm camp my mother-in-law went looking for him. And later we learnt -- I told the truth. We didn't know until that point in time that they were executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Islamcevic. My last question, to clarify something that was not quite clear yesterday, in connection with a question that my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman put to you. It has to do with this statement of the 15th of February 1995. And in answer to a question by the President as to whether that statement was typed out on the same day and whether you signed it the same day, you stated that it wasn't written the same day but that you wrote the statement yourself and signed it and that after that, the statement was typed out and transformed into this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Zecevic, he never said that he wrote the statement himself. He said that there was a handwritten version of it which he signed on the same day it was written, but this particular version, the typed-out version, was handed to him two or three days later and he signed that too. That's what he said. But he never said that he drew up one himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- if I may, if it please it is Court, he -- what I am asking actually the witness is the fact that I only found out last night when I was checking the transcript that this part which he actually said in Serbian did not show up in the transcript. That is why I'm trying to clarify this situation. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you understand the question. You --

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need. I understand, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain, sir. I'll be glad to. I think that I correctly stated that at that point in time and even today I didn't know the personal identification numbers, that they were not my product.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That was not my question, sir. I'm just asking you this.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything else I can confirm in this court. I said everything that is contained in that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just asking you one thing: Is it true that while you were having that interview, a statement was compiled that was handwritten?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was read and signed, and that is the content in the version that you have before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This handwritten statement, was it written by you?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not me. I dictated it. I was narrating the course of events and answering questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You dictated this to somebody else who wrote it out by hand.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to someone else, but an official person, a representative of the competent institution in charge of taking a statement from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And after that, you signed this handwritten statement.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A couple of days later you were called in. The statement had been typed out. And then you signed it. And this is the statement shown to you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I am saying that this statement is mine with the exception of the personal identification numbers. And not Mr. Zijad, as your colleague wanted us to believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. We have three, four minutes before we break. Is there a re-examination? I would imagine so. How much time do you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: 15, 20 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we better break. We'll break and -- we are going to have a 15-minute break now. We will resume at 4.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Mr. Islamcevic, if you could direct your mind to the meeting on the 19th of August of 1992 with Mr. Sergio de Mello in Topusko. It was put to you that you had spoken at that meeting about members of the 3rd Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade. Do you recall that question during cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is today, Mr. Cayley. No?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was a very simple question. And you retorted immediately. You said that that formed part of the 6th Krajina Brigade. You took objection at the way the question was being put to you, suggesting that this had nothing to do with the 6th Krajina Brigade, and you said, "No, it was the 6th Krajina Brigade." This is -- if you want, we can go back to the part of the transcript, if you can locate it, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please just remind me of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can easily find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Let me try and remind him, Your Honour. And if we can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Then we'll find it in the transcript and read it back to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall speaking at that meeting in Topusko about the 3rd Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the part when I -- well, you say a private meeting, but it wasn't a private meeting. When the two Muslims -- when we two Muslims remained there and when I mentioned the actions that had already been taken in Trnovo and in Hrustovo. Is that the part you are referring to? Is that the part about which you want to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. Now, I'm looking at your statement here, and I won't put it in front of you, but you said to Sergio -- you spoke to him about Vrhpolje and Hrustovo communes and the crimes committed there. And when I pointed out Vrhpolje, I made a gesture with the other hand of cutting his throat. Sergio said, "I know. I told them mass execution by shooting there, Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, and that people were allegedly put in a house and the house set on fire. I also said that in Vrhpolje men were stopped on the bridge, killed, and their bodies thrown into the River Sana. I knew about what was going on in the town and in the villages because every week I had meetings with representatives from other communes at the marketplace."

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just read out is correct, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, in the next part of your statement it goes like this: "Sergio asked who did this. I said that according to my knowledge, the perpetrators were members of the 3rd Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade stationed in Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct too.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How do you know that the perpetrators of these crimes were members of the 3rd Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this and I base my knowledge on several sources. One of the sources is Muslim. People who recognised certain men -- certain people in the town, certain people from the town. And the second source is a Serbian one, which says that one old man was the first person to open fire and that the army had nothing else to do -- could not do anything else -- all they could do was to clean -- clean Hrustovo. I said that in my statement, and this was the justification they provided for the cleaning. And I said that among other things, this information was from a civilian representative, a Serbian at that time, a representative for Pobrijezje, Podlug, and Demisovci. His name was Mr. Hasikovic [phoen], Pero Vujkovic [phoen]. Similarly I knew that our neighbours from Podlug belonged to the 3rd Battalion. I also knew -- I also knew that because part of the 3rd Battalion -- and surprisingly I can't remember who the leaders were -- I knew that part of the 3rd Battalion was also located in the social centre in the local commune of Pobrijezje. So I was able to see those people who were coming and going, and I remember -- I can remember a certain man, someone called Cemkovic [phoen], who was a guard of the B Battalion, someone who was too old for combat and he made use of the opportunity to fire a few shots from the street and to fire these shots at the window of my father's house. There is no doubt that the 3rd Battalion -- that parts of the 3rd Battalion took action in Hrustovo and participated in the cleaning of Hrustovo and in everything that occurred up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think Mr. Basara was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, you were similarly asked today about the individuals who moved members of the Serb population from Mahala, living in Pobrijezje, the individuals who subsequently moved those citizens out of the Sanski Most municipality altogether. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had an exchange with the gentleman over there about that subject. So the expelled -- the Muslims expelled from the Mahala settlement, the Mahala neighbourhood, spent a certain time in the local commune of Pobrijezje. I had the figure written down, and I can confidently state that the lower part of Pobrijezje -- soldiers took people away from the lower part of Pobrijezje. And in the upper part, on the bridge, which is further up from my house, I didn't see that but I had information with regard to their departure because some people knew Njunja, just as I did. They knew him and his men. I can quite claim -- I can certainly claim when we are speaking about this convoy that both were engaged in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, the soldiers that you saw in the lower part of your commune gathering the people to move them out, did you know to which unit those soldiers belonged?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milorad Cucak, known as Adi, born in Podlug, son of Rade -- son of Rade, a man who in 1992 at an official meeting in Podlug said, "Thank God that the time has come in which I can see -- a time has come in which I can say that I'm a son of a Chetnik." On that day he was in front of my father's house. He was on the road, N-15, the road from Prijedor to Sanski Most. I saw him and heard him hurrying people up and shouting, and I also heard in a more positive context -- I heard a captain who had left the family of my wife. I knew a lawyer from the Sip in Sana, Jovo, called the poor man. I can't remember his surname. He was at the door of Hasic Teufik's house, 15 metres as the crow flies from my house. And there were refugees too, refugees from Mahala, the woman's relatives. And I saw that gentleman there too and some other people.
