And certainly some people who belonged to the 3rd Battalion were in Pobrijezje on that day. There was no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And that was the 3rd Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the 3rd Battalion of the 3rd Brigade [as said] members of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion of the 3rd Brigade or the 3rd Battalion of the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact the previous intervention was -- it was put to him that the 3rd Battalion was part of the territorial forces. And he stated that it certainly wasn't, it was part of the 6th Brigade, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If these three statements could be placed in front of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you will have gathered that it's basically been put to you that one of your statements -- at least one of your statements you did not sign yourself. So what I would like to do is to get through each of your statements and have you look at every one of your signatures and state to the Judges whether or not that is your signature. Do you have your statement of the 13th of February of 1995 in front of you? This is the statement that you gave to the Bosnian authorities. It's countersigned by a man called Josip Ljubez.

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you look at the bottom right-hand corner of that statement where it says "Besim Islamcevic." It's typewritten. And there's a signature over the top of that typewritten name. Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that certainly is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you now look at the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness has been asked these questions by me. He's been asked these questions by Your Honour. I don't think it's appropriate redirect. He's been asked and answered. He's said it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I mean, I'm -- I was pretty sure that the re-examination would have concentrated on these three documents. So I'm going to allow the question and then we'll take it up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you look at the next page, again where it says in the bottom right-hand corner "Islamcevic Besim." Do you see your signature underneath the typewritten version of your name?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could create certain doubts, but given the situation at the time that I signed this and the condition I was in -- and yesterday I gave four versions of my signature. But given -- taking this into account, it's my signature. But I did say with regard to the personal identification numbers that these were things that I could not accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's -- he's mixing up. He's gone to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the signatures, Mr. Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are still -- Mr. Islamcevic, please pay attention. We are still referring to the first document that Mr. Cayley referred you to -- asked you to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think he has that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is the statement of the 13th, a two-page statement of the 13th of February --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have answered that question, and I said that that was my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But the question related only to the signature on the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No. I did ask about the signature on the second page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But that's when he mixed up and he started --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Talking about the content of the second statement. If you want, I'll ask that question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If you look at the second page of your statement of the 13th of February of 1995, that is your signature; correct?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: But you stated at the time you were in a -- a fairly fragile physical and mental condition, correct, when you signed this?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said with regard to the time spent in Sanski Most and going out into the territory, I said that the situation and the psychological states that people found themselves in, it would vary. So it's perhaps not identical. And I told the Trial Chamber and the Defence -- I showed them four versions of my signature, and I provided them with these versions for them to examine. There's no doubt about this. On the 13th of February, yes, that is my very own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the last question in respect of this statement of the 13th of February, which you've read previously: Are the contents -- or at the time that you signed this statement, did you believe the contents to be true?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If we could now -- if you could put that statement to one side --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Unless, Mr. President, you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I have a simple question. With regard to this first statement of the 13th of February, what was the procedure used? Was it like when you were interrogated by Mr. Zijad Ibric? In other words, did you have an interrogation and a statement -- handwritten statement prepared which you signed and then you were asked to return to the office to sign the typewritten statement? Was it like that, or was it different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the statement wasn't written in advance. It was written down on a sheet of paper that I signed. Later on it was typed out and read back to me -- it was read out and it was then signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it read out by Mr. Josip Ljubez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. At that time I didn't know the person, but he introduced himself, said his name was Josip Ljubez, and in the course of a conversation I heard people calling him Josip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But this document that we have here was not signed by you on the same day you were interrogated by him. No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was it signed by you on the same day that Mr. Zijad Ibric asked you to go back to the office to sign this statement that he had prepared for you to sign? Did you go, in other words, once back to the office or twice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't sign this typed statement up until the time when I gave this statement on the 15th of February. So a few days later I signed this one too, the first statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When you signed the two statements, did you sign them on the same day or on different days? You were interrogated definitely on different days.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You signed them on different days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Not on the same day. On different days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you went back to the office where these statements were twice and not once. Just to sign the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can you now look at the statement of the 15th of February. Do you have that in front of you? And if you could just look at every single page of that statement. There are six pages on which your signature appear. And tell me when you've finished reading through. Have you finished reading it through?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Is that your signature on every page?

utterances.speaker: BESIM ISLAMCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to say I know that on that morning before I went to sign this statement which Zijad Ibric asked for I had solved my housing problems in Travnik and I was in a good mood. I know that we had -- had coffee and I had a look at this, and I had an objection to make with regard to the personal identification numbers. I said with regard to the personal identification numbers that everything else that the statement contained was something that I had said and that I accepted it as such. I was told that this was no problem. And then I quickly signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Islamcevic, that brings us to the end of your testimony here. And on behalf of the Tribunal, I would like to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial. You will now be escorted out of the courtroom by the usher, and you will be given all --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, would you allow me to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Certainly. But let me finish first. You will be escorted out of the courtroom by --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And taken back to your hotel and given all the assistance you require to return back to your country. And we wish you a safe journey back home. Yes, you may say whatever you like provided it's short. You may sit down. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to thank you and your assistants. I would like to thank you for making it possible for me to come here and for having listened to my testimony over these days. I would like to thank the Tribunal, the Tribunal in The Hague for making it possible for me to come here. I would like to thank the United Nations for having made this possible. I would also like to greet counsel for the Defence and to wish them a lot of happiness and a long life, and this especially concerns Mr. Brdjanin and Mr. Talic, the clients. I hope that their health will be good and that they will have a long life. And that when conditions are right they will be able to return to their homes and to their families. It was an honour for me to be able to meet Mr. Cayley. I thank him, and I hope that he will have a lot of success in his work and that he will have a lot of success in his family life. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Islamcevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose the next witness is still sick.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, yes. I mean, he was never -- it's not really sick. It's just that he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He hasn't recovered.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He needs time to recover, I think, from seeing Mr. -- Mr. Nicholls. Thank you. So Your Honour, can I deal with the -- with a number of matters. The first matter I think we need to go into private session for because it was something that was raised in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We don't want to be in private session for me to say this. I just want to be in the record that I have permission to make disclosures to Mr. Shellow regarding the matters that have been discussed in private session today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You certainly have, Mr. Ackerman. And in fact, if it can be of any help to you, we can have this part of the transcript copied to you -- or you can -- you can -- and fax it over to him --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll have it at the end of the day and I'll simply fax it to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to leave the handwriting aspect to the end, because I think that's going to be more contentious matters, although this one may be too. Dates. And Your Honour, I'm sorry, I scrawled -- I suddenly realised I scrawled some notes without realising on the back of Your Honour's calendar. Mr. Ackerman asked for a break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Well, first of all, it's the principle. Mr. Ackerman is working on the principle of four weeks on, one week off. I'm -- I made this point last time. Your Honour, I'm not in favour on behalf of the Prosecution of an automatic week off. I mean, if Your Honours are, then I'll -- I won't bother any further. But it seems to me that there's a lot of ground still to cover in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't been working on a basis of four weeks off and one week off.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's what Mr. Ackerman told me he's working on the basis of, and that's what he's put into his schedule. Anyhow, can I just make the point that -- that October the 24th is a UN holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now I need a diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, do you have -- perhaps you can print out.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But in fact at this moment all I wanted to do -- we'll put our suggestions in then. Is ask Your Honours for the dates again. Your Honour has already given us a couple of dates when you are off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Taya and myself require basically not to be engaged here the week which -- in November which ends on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that's the whole week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I basically need the Friday before the 16th. That's the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Judge Taya needs the 14th. So I would say --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So that week is out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would say the whole week if that's convenient for you. If it's not convenient for you, then we can have a Monday and steal a day or two there --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Those are the only dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise it will not be before January when I hope to become a grandpa that I will need to go to Malta.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour that, assists. And I think all the courts are adjourning for the -- for the Christmas recess --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- on the 14th. The last sitting day is the 14th. Except for, I understand that maybe Milosevic is carrying on. Your Honour, there is -- is there a plenary in December? That's the only other thing I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. There will be a plenary. And it will be roughly -- if we are stopping on the 14th -- the 14th is what day?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the plenary would probably be the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a Saturday in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So it will be the 12th and the 13th probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, don't quote me, because it's something that the President decides upon, not me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But usually the practice has been for a Thursday and a Friday. Usually it has been Wednesday, Thursday, Friday. And we normally end our works on Thursday. This time it's -- instead of going to be Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, in July it's going to be Thursday and Friday. And then December I would assume that it will be the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's -- Your Honour, that's very helpful. At least we know we'll have to work around those dates. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, we'll come back to this on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we also intend, unless there is any special reason why not to, to resume the beginning of the last week in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the 26th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think so we -- again, all the courts are doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's very helpful. If we can come back to this on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, as far as we are concerned, we do not have any requirements. What we expect you to do is to try and accommodate each other. We realise that this is not an ordinary case. It's heavy. And it takes its toil. I mean, I guess sometimes I can see it on myself when I look in the mirror at the end of the day or in the beginning of the day, and sometimes I see it on your faces as well. So ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, I think all -- all that -- my concern is, and it always has been, is that given that all teams now have two counsel, it should be possible perhaps not to have full weeks off -- obviously days will have to be taken off and the right. But that's another matter. Your Honour, that brings me on to the next aspect, which is we have today filed -- we have today filed the motion for protective measures for all the remaining municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's good.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That was filed this afternoon. It includes in them witnesses who we are anticipating we will be seeking to attend under Rule 92. Your Honour said we should repeat that -- I mean, Your Honour said we should put that in the motion, but we'll just repeat it again. But that is now filed -- or should be by -- or should have been by 4.00. Your Honour, Mr. Mayhew, he was one of the Rule 92 -- the witnesses we wished to tender under Rule 92. And Madam Fauveau objected, and it was said he had to attend for cross-examination. Your Honour, in actual fact we will be calling him live because having heard from Mr. McLeod, Mr. Mayhew can fill in gaps that Mr. McLeod couldn't. So he's going to be called in both this and the Stakic case. I anticipate in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, I can now turn to what I'm concerned about, and that is as a result of the cross-examination of this witness today and Adil Draganovic. Your Honour, the matter arose first with him, although I think another intervening witness may have been asked without it, but I'm not positive. In that, Your Honours will recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. There was another witness who was --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There was no problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it was abandoned at that stage, as far as I recall that line of defence. But it began with Judge Draganovic, it being suggested to him that a particular signature on one of the statements taken from other witnesses at which he'd been present was not his, that it differed in the method of the signature. And the end result was -- and Your Honours may recall that was not a particularly happy day when he left. The suggestion was clearly that someone else unknown had forged the judge's signature on a statement of another witness. That -- that witness was then called and gave evidence to the effect that the judge had been there when that statement was taken by AID. There isn't and never has been, as I understand it, one iota of evidence on which the Defence base this suggestion that they've been making that the signature of a witness, whether it is Mr. Draganovic or this witness, that is not his signature, other than to the Defence's untutored eye it looks different. And one of the rules certainly that we apply in my jurisdiction, and I think Your Honour's, and most jurisdictions is that laymen are not and cannot be handwriting experts unless they're familiar with the disputed handwriting or have seen it actually being written in front of them. And so the first point that I want to make about this is I'm not at all clear on what possible basis, on what evidential basis these suggestions are being made. But can I -- can I move to what is the next problem. The response of Mr. Draganovic was that this was his signature, that he signed in a number of different ways, which may not be a phenomenon unknown to most of us. He's been asked to supply samples of all his type of signatures. Let us suppose that Your Honour orders or Mr. Ackerman obtains permission to instruct a handwriting expert and the expert looks at it, if he's able to, because one is a photocopy and one is an original signature, and says, "Well, I'm not sure one way or the other." Or even, let's say, he says, "Well, it doesn't look to me -- I am -- as far as I can be certain, it doesn't look like the same signature." Where exactly does that leave us? Because the witness himself is saying, "It is my signature. I was there. I did sign." And indeed in this case, as I say, that was supported by the person whose statement that it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why earlier on I told you I'm not that much worried about Draganovic as such, because we have his statement on oath that despite what appearances may or might be, that is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour, supported, for what it's worth, by the witness himself whose statement it was saying he was there. Your Honour, that's why my concern is arising about this, because as I said before, all of this is happening in open court and these allegations are being made which are serious allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But there was the allegation -- the initial allegation, Ms. Korner, was -- and I'm just saying this as I understood it to be. If I'm making a mistake, Mr. Ackerman I'm sure will correct me. But the impression I got at the time was that it was being suggested that there could have possibly been some sort of conspiracy between Mr. Draganovic and Mr. Ibric in procuring evidence in this legal fashion, manner. If I am misinterpreting you, Mr. Ackerman, please do correct me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's certainly what I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't had the -- Mr. Ibric come -- come here to give evidence, so I would say nothing that could compromise or benefit Mr. Ibric. But Mr. Draganovic, who was one of the persons against whom these insinuations were being -- were being made -- and I am using the word "insinuation" in a innocent way and not in -- did state, make affirmations on oath which would a priori exclude what was being imputed against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, may I say that's the second -- I know I'm dealing with a limited aspect at the moment of what is this allegation of a conspiracy. Without at the moment any foundation having been laid to show there is such a conspiracy -- and Your Honours, certainly we have no intention of calling Mr. Ibric to give evidence until there's some foundation being laid to show that there's the slightest truth in any of these allegations. Because Your Honour, one of the things that this is doing -- and this is my concern -- is it is distracting attention from what are the real issues in the case. To what issue in the case does -- and I'm limiting it now to handwriting. Forget about -- of course the issue is that these documents that we have produced -- received from AID are no some way forgeries, and Your Honour, the burden is always on us to show Your Honour that -- Your Honours that it is not a forgery. But this question of the handwriting. To what issue in the case does it go? Because these witnesses have testified on oath as to what they say happened, which is contained within the contents of their statements. It has not been suggested to a single one of these witnesses on the major aspect to which they've been called to testify that in some way they're lying about what they say happened. So in one sense it could be said to say what is in the statement signed by them or not signed, as the allegation is at the moment, is only relevant if it's inconsistent with the testimony that they give or in some cases if there's a suggestion of recent fabrication to show that it's consistent with what they said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not going to comment on that. I will leave -- leave it to the Defence to make submissions upon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because there is much to say in favour and beyond what -- in favour and against, but also beyond what ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, all that I'm concerned about is that it's come up again today -- is firstly, how far are Your Honours going to allow this to extend? Can I say that -- and if -- if I finish then Your Honour can tell me -- if. If Your Honour does feel that the Defence are entitled to take this line, although as we submit it has absolutely nothing to do with the issues in this case, which is whether or not these people who are before Your Honours are telling Your Honours the truth and are accurate, of course -- whether or not, now that a second set of handwriting has been demanded the Court should take the action, because I don't know that Mr. Ackerman has done anything about it. Your Honour raised it -- of saying, "All right. If you, Your Honours, think that it is relevant and that something needs to be done about it, well, then a graphologist ought to be instructed straight away let's deal with that and that may bring an end to it." Your Honours, those are the matters that I want to raise. Because it seems to me that we're spending an awful lot of time and indeed making a lot of public accusations which at the moment there's foundation made as to relevance or to what issue they go, or indeed if there's any foundation for making a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let me before I give the floor to either Mr. Ackerman or to Mr. Zecevic tell you something. Having been a Defence counsel myself, I'm pretty sure that both Mr. Ackerman and both Mr. Zecevic, when they raised the issue or tried to put in doubt the authenticity of a signature, particularly of a witness who can very easily say, "It may look different, but that is mine," are doing so with their eyes wide open. In other words, they know that if they do it once and they get nowhere, they do it a second time and they get nowhere, they do it a third time and they get nowhere, at the end of the day it could turn out to work against them. So I'm saying this because I was a Defence lawyer and I know that each and every Defence counsel will go this far but not beyond. And in fact you would notice that in the three witnesses that we have had so far, where in the case of Adil Draganovic there was certainly one of the signatures or more than one of the signatures on the face of it that did not really look or resemble the other signatures. But the difference was not much. And when he tendered -- gave us specimens of his signature, one could possibly also see -- see clearer. Second, the witness that we've had here -- I think -- I think it was pretty plain sailing and it was not taken at any -- to any distance by the Defence, and I would have exactly -- done exactly the same thing. The witness we had yesterday, when I, as I usually do, was going through the documentation that you had provided us with -- I mean, if there was anything that struck me from the word go was that the signature on the statement of the 15th of February had absolutely nothing visibly to do with the signatures appearing on the other -- on the other two documents. And I would have downgraded my esteem of Mr. Ackerman considerably had he not brought it up, especially if he had not brought it up considering that we are talking again of the same person against whom he had made an insinuation in the first place when he was dealing with Adil. So if you ask me at this particular stage whether at -- now this Chamber will close the door upon the Defence and preclude them from -- from proceeding along these lines any further, for the time being certainly not. Certainly not. Because first of all, it's -- I mean, anything can happen on the face of this -- of this earth, and it's not to be ruled out that we may not be talking of a fabrication. And if a witness realises that his signature has been forged but it is -- it would be very much counterproductive for him to admit that and have the contents of that statement thrown out completely when it's to his advantage, it's -- it's something that we have to keep constantly in mind. We are an open book -- we -- in other words, at this particular point in time, we do not draw conclusions. I may in my mind have come to certain conclusions with regard to this witness that we had today. I may have come to certain conclusions with regard to Adil Draganovic. But I don't know what to expect next. The next witness -- we have, for example, the next witness, 7.59 -- 7.59 has also made a statement to Mr. Ibric. And you look at the two signatures, the ones on the statement released to the Prosecution, and you look at the statements released to Mr. Ibric - and I don't know. I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is doing what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Exactly. But I suppose at this stage you are doing exactly the same thing. You wouldn't have bothered about comparing signatures had this incident of Mr. Draganovic not come up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We haven't been comparing signatures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But we have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the matter has been brought up. And until we are satisfied that this is either a -- an approach that the Defence should -- it's high time that they drop or that it is something that should be investigated as we -- as we go along and conclusions reached then on the ensemble of the evidence that is brought forward, we -- I don't think we are in a position to take a decision. What I can be clear about is a simple matter, that basically the rule is that we would stop the Defence if questions are put to the witness based on mere suspicions, not based on anything - at least prima facie.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- I'm afraid that's the point then, isn't it? Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Okay. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But if the -- on the face of it the signature of Mr. Islamcevic on the three documents was identical and Mr. Ackerman tried to question -- question it, I'm not saying that I would have necessarily stopped him, but I would have certainly drawn his attention to the fact that on the face of it the three signatures were identical.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And therefore no insinuation should be made any further with regard to that particular --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know. But Your Honour, that's -- that's really -- I say this with the greatest of respect -- what none of us should be doing. Because in fact it is just as conceivable that a signature that looks identical can be forged. We're making -- Your Honours are, Mr. Ackerman is - because as I say, he's got no evidence as I understand it to suggest this - a value judgement based on a -- an ignorance, if you like -- or because we're not experts, of handwriting. And Your Honour, that's the difficulty. Your Honour is saying if it looks the same, I'm going to stop Mr. Ackerman, but if it's looks different, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. If it look it is same, I'm going to ask Mr. Ackerman why he is questioning it. And if Mr. Ackerman says because I just have a suspicion, I will stop him. If Mr. Ackerman, however -- I'm sorry I'm referring to Mr. Ackerman. It could be Mr. Zecevic or Mr. Trbojevic. It could be anyone. But unfortunately I don't think that we have that situation. We have a situation where however fragile it might appear to be, there is an allegation that we could have a massive fraud having taken place.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The massive fraud being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A massive fraud is what Mr. Ackerman hinted at, is not in a position to prove, is awaiting information -- further information from Sarajevo about, and matters on which you have four boxes or five boxes of material that has arrived that has not been yet vetted and has not, of course, yet been translated or disclosed to the Defence. So at this point in time you will understand that I am not going to close doors. I am going to leave all options open.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I just want to point out that Mr. Ackerman launched this particular attack before there was any arrests had taken place of any other people in AID in these matters, which are unconnected with this case. But Your Honour, all that I am saying -- and I'm not going to pursue this any longer, because at the moment I can see Your Honours are against me -- is this: That it is not in our submission proper to start cross-examining witnesses and taking samples of handwriting from witnesses without, A, some foundation - and by that I don't mean simply having a look at it and saying the signature looks different - or secondly, at least, dealing with it. Your Honour, I think what must happen is that if these signatures are being taken for the purposes -- and they're now court exhibits -- for the purposes of handwriting comparison, then Your Honour can order such handwriting comparison to take place as soon as possible. The signatures can be -- you the Judges can order handwriting comparisons with the signatures that are now in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman. Before I answer that, if I answer it. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to be quite brief. I think to some extent Ms. Korner is handicapped by not having been here yesterday, and I'll get to that in a moment. We were frankly -- Your Honour, we were discussing this last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And one of the things that we are concerned about is that with this situation in existence regarding the suspicions about Mr. Ibric and AID, we were all somewhat concerned that when you look at these documents, as Your Honour did, it jumps out at you that the signatures on these three documents appear dramatically different. And bearing in mind the -- the obligations of people who prosecute, we were concerned as to why the Prosecution clearly did not ask this witness before he came into this courtroom if these were his signatures. It would seem to me if the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're taking it for granted that they didn't, and that you are imputing to the Prosecution a shortcoming. I don't know what the Prosecution did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I don't either. But I think it's clear, and that's where I get to my second point. When I asked the witness yesterday - and Your Honour knows this well, and Mr. Cayley know this is well - when I asked him yesterday to look at the document of 15 February 1995 and tell me if it was his signature that appeared on those documents, his response was something to the effect "I can't be sure." That was the response. Now, that gives me a basis to go a bit further, it seems to me, and certainly justifies to some extent what I've been doing in the past with regard to that matter. It certainly gives me a basis for requesting that he give us some exemplars. We have been challenging many of these witnesses on what it is they're testifying about, not just signatures but what it is they contend the facts were. And Your Honours know that. It's -- that's not the only thing they're being challenged about. Now, let's assume that I contend that with two of these witnesses it appears on the face of it that what -- their names signed were signed by different people. If that's the way it appears on the face, and I don't ask that. I just forget it. And then in the Defence case I bring a handwriting expert and say, "Did you compare these signatures? "Yes, I did." "Are they the same?." "No they were signed by different people." Then what I would get from Ms. Korner is Rule 90(H) requires that you should have put that to the witness if that's what you were going to do. So I have to put it to the witness under Rule 90(H). I have to say, "Are these your signatures?" I have to do that. Now, I haven't said to one of these witnesses, "Isn't that a forgery? Did someone else sign that?" I haven't done that. I've asked them if it was their signature. And I've had them sign papers. With Draganovic I showed him blown-ups of the signatures and I said, "Which one of these is not yours?" I did do that. But I don't think there's anything wrong with what I've been doing. I don't think there's anything improper with what I've been doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber doesn't think that what you have been doing is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We looked at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm being very blunt on that, especially having seen the specimens that the last witness gave us yesterday. And this is why I am -- I am definitely not closing doors for the time being, because if it's still difficult to find an explanation for the diversity in the signatures upon those three documents that we saw during his testimony, I am absolutely -- I feel at a complete loss when I try to compare the signature which he had before him -- in front of him there, the signature on the second of those statements, the one co-signed by Mr. Ibric, and the specimen signatures that he gave us yesterday. And this is the problem that the Trial Chamber has. The Trial Chamber cannot operate on suspicions and will not allow the proceedings to deviate based on mere suspicions. But on the -- on the other hand, what do we have? We have three statements containing three signatures, two of which are seemingly identical. And okay, we are not calligraphic experts or graphologists, we are not. But we operate first and foremost on the basis of what is apparent. And then we go further, if there is need, and then we resort to experts. But on the face of it, what we had were three statements, each containing a signature. One of, which did not at least on the face of it, at least as it appeared, correspond to the appearance of the other two signatures or the signatures appearing on the other two documents. I ask you does that signature correspond to the eight signatures -- that specimen signatures that Mr. Islamcevic gave us yesterday. None of us is an expert, but on the basis of what we saw would you say that it is a case of appointing a graphologist -- a calligraphic expert to -- to decide this for us or to give us an expert opinion? Well, it depends. If there is a request from the Defence, we will go ahead with that. If it's -- there is no request from the Defence, we will not take the initiative.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before she does. At this point I'm -- ordinarily this is the way it would work: The way it would work is that I would get the specimens from the witness, like I have, that I would find an expert that I would get authorisation from the Registry to retain that expert, that I would submit the materials to that expert, that that expert would submit a report, that I would name that person as an expert who would be testifying in the Defence of my case, and that the report would be delivered to the Prosecutor as the Rules require and that person would be called as a witness in my case. That's the way it would ordinarily work. When I wanted to read some documents to you just as retaliation for Ms. Korner reading documents to you, I was told that I could only do that in the Defence case. I think I can only bring an expert on handwriting in the Defence case too. So to somehow speed this up -- I don't know how. If Your Honours want to -- want to have me try to do this more quickly and bring an expert in out of order -- a Defence expert in the middle of the Prosecutor's case, I wouldn't mind doing that. It might -- it might actually solve something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Our point -- our point is that I don't know if we have come to that stage where we need to appoint an -- a graphologist. I don't know. And we don't have a request at this -- at this point in time. And I would imagine that a request would only be forthcoming after one has evaluated the substance of the evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have been in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But there are many things to say, Mr. Ackerman. I mean, if you look at statements tendered to the Prosecution, they are professionally prepared and presented. Each page is initialed by not -- by all the persons -- all the persons involved. So we're talking of one, two, three, sometimes even four persons. If we're talking of the statements to Mr. Ibric and to whoever, you -- you look at them. I mean, at least the copies that I have you have the first page signed by both of them, the second page I have a signature of just the person interviewed, the third the same, the fourth the same, the fifth the same, and then on the sixth I have both signatures. But this is -- this is what I have. It may be the result of -- of photocopying process, but this is what we have. And I don't think it is, because on the first page they are aligned on the same line; on the second and subsequent pages, the signature or countersignature of Mr. Ibric is -- is possible. So in theory there is the possibility of having a person sign one page and sign another page or -- and replace those in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, can I perhaps put it this way: Let us say for the sake of this argument that Mr. Ackerman's suggestions - and I beg leave to differ with him - he actually put in terms to the judge that that wasn't his signature. None of this "Is this your signature?" And I see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, he did --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I mean, let's not get away from that. That was all out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He did -- you did definitely put to the judge that it wasn't his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, let us say that just for the sake of this discussion, Mr. Ackerman's absolutely right, and that for some reason or another Mr. Ibric filled in this man's name on the statement that he undoubtedly made but didn't sign for some reason and so Mr. Ibric signed it. To what actual issue in this case is that going to go as respects the witness? Because the witness has given you -- and this particular witness -- I wasn't here. I did actually see what was happening yesterday because I was watching it -- the witness gave evidence of deportation of everything that he said had happened to him. That wasn't challenged. That's in his statement. So where does -- where does the fact go that he may not have signed that one page of his statement or whatever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. Two things were challenged, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The other thing is that even given that that is his signature, the statement is not entirely his.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was another thing that was -- that was put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which he objected other than the personal identification numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There -- we did not have the opportunity, neither because the matter was not prosecuted any further by the -- either by the Defence or by the Prosecution as to the -- the rest of the details of -- of the statement, because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm pretty sure that if you had gone through that statement sentence after sentence, there would have -- there would still have come out certain other detail that is must have been filled -- filled in, not just -- I'm pretty sure that if I had asked the witness "Let's go through all the persons that are mentioned here" and Mr. X, son of -- if there are 30 persons mentioned with the father's name, et cetera, I'm pretty sure that at the end of the day he would have given us half of them but not the whole 30 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I find that slightly worrying, if I may say so. Because if Your Honours are going to take that view, that there is something, then there is an obligation on Your Honours to ask these questions. As it is, there is an unanswered question. The Defence dump it, if I can put it colloquially because they don't think it's getting them anywhere. Of course we don't -- but if Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do feel Your Honours are the triers of the fact. That rather than a doubt or a suspicion lingering, Your Honours should ask those questions or make it clear to us for the Prosecution that you expect us to go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. Ms. Korner, if no questions are forthcoming, then the Trial Chamber will take the statement -- that statement as it -- as it -- as it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, exactly, Your Honour. That's what I mean. And if the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that my hunch is that if one had tried to take that statement one by one -- sentence by sentence, the probability is what exactly happens in the case of all the interrogations that I have had to deal with in my -- in my career. When you have a system whereby everything is tape recorded and you have the question which is reproduced and the answer that is reproduced, then that problem becomes much -- much, much less. When you have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the questions tape-recorded and then someone creates the statement, then you have if you try to really extract the whole truth and all the details, you are going to -- and that's -- Mr. Ackerman tried one yesterday and he failed when he tried to get the infamous --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. I saw that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He failed. But I mean, that's his problem. He tried it and he got nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. That is the whole point, isn't it? That there is no real -- we all know, of course, when police officers take statements what comes out sometimes is not the actual words of the witness but the words used by a police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I get.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Absolutely. But what is being suggested here, Your Honour, is that it's not just that the police officer has used phraseology which weren't the witness's own but actually convey what the witness meant. It's suggested, as I say, without any foundation that I can see that parts of the statement have been put in by Mr. Ibric - which they have -- the personal identification numbers - but it's going further. That's the underlying, that somehow or other, because there was part put in by Mr. Ibric, somehow that statement is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's a supposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. But that's -- that's the implied suggestion that that's why this whole business of the signatures and all that is being brought up. But, Your Honour, the witnesses are giving evidence before you of what they say happened. And when I say it's not being challenged, that the actual fact that this man says "My father was murdered," or huge amounts of people -- there's no challenge being put to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course not, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But then -- Your Honour, that's my point. I'll come back to it for the last time. What is the issue in the case to which the signing or non-signing of this statement by the various -- the various statements by the witnesses goes to? If it's a matter of credit, then answers going to credit are final. You can't call evidence on extraneous issues. Your Honour, we could actually spend a very long time in Mr. Ackerman's case listening to handwriting experts I suppose theoretically on whether or not a particular statement contained the signature of this particular man, and how would that help Your Honours in deciding whether or not the allegations made by the Prosecution through the witnesses of whole-scale murder, of destruction, and whatever are true. That's -- that's the only -- the only reason I'm raising this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It might have absolutely no bearing on that. It could well be. But this is why I premised everything on something fundamental. That -- I believe that Defence counsel know perfectly well that the moment they decide to engage the Chamber -- the Trial Chamber in this sphere, that they are doing this with their eyes open. Because I mean if they can manage to prove, without having a burden of proof -- I mean, if they manage to create a scenario on the basis of which doubt is put or is inserted in -- in the case of the Prosecution, that's one thing. If they are not successful in this exercise, it could have the opposite effect; it could bounce back on the Prosecution -- on the Defence. I mean, I'm saying this because we are still at pretty much -- I don't know if Zijad Ibric, for example, is a person that is only involved in the Sanski Most municipality or he may be involved in other municipalities. I haven't got a clue. I haven't got an idea. I don't know if the suspicions of the Defence are restricted, limited to Mr. Zijad Ibric or whether they extend also to other persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, as far as I understand, it's AID as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. But I say I don't know because so far we have had a -- a statement to that effect but we haven't had evidence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are -- we are still waiting for that. So I would give the Defence credit that so far the only two instances in which they raised the matter both involved a person, the credibility of whom or the integrity of whom they seemed to be attacking - that's Zijad Ibric within an AID framework - and they raised the matter in only two cases where at least on the face of it there was something to say. Now, in the first case we had the witness categorically stating that the signature that was being put to him as not being his was his, followed by the production, bringing forward of the other witness who confirmed that the signature was his and that of Adil Draganovic and Ibric were theirs and it was -- they were put in his presence. That chapter was closed. We didn't have the same problem with a subsequent witness that had also released a statement to Mr. Ibric, or it seemed to start but stopped -- was nipped in the bud by the Defence itself. I mean, never went any further than that. We had the second case yesterday. And on the face of it, at least, without going into -- into details or without purporting to be an expert on -- in handwriting, on the face of it justified the Defence at least raising the matter. I would have raised it; for sure. This is the -- this is the situation. Now, if there's going to be a third case, I don't know. If it's going -- there's going to be a fourth case, I don't know. And what's going to happen if there is a third, fourth, and subsequent cases, I don't know. I mean, there is another witness coming forward very soon. I don't think we will have a problem, but that's because I am just -- I am just looking. Mr. Ackerman may -- may have a deeper insight or more information or information that I certainly don't have and question that signature too. How do I know? This is the situation. I don't think that we are -- or we have arrived at a stage or we have been dealing with a case where stopping the Defence from proceeding any further was called for. I mean, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right. Well, Your Honour, I've made -- I've made my submission, and I'm not going to take up any more of the Court's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. Any submissions from --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorely tempted, but I think I'd better not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are you still in the mood for reading to us, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I took the view that Mr. Ackerman was going to walk out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think it's quarter to 6.00 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I think let's join with Mr. Ackerman and we all --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I haven't brought any with me, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I want to make sure, Ms. Korner, that we don't have any health problems with the next witness tomorrow. And for that reason, I would ask you to make sure with the Victims and Witnesses Section to be on the alert, be present here, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it going to be a closed session or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he's in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Closed session, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that's even more important.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. He is closed session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's even more important that we have someone. Because if we were in open session, it would be all transparent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's in closed session, I don't want anything to happen with the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the lingering suspicion that we did not take precautions or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, we'll certainly -- but I'm told at the moment his treatment -- his course and treatment has halted. So I think it's just a question of tiredness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. But I'm sure you understood what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks. And we will resume tomorrow at 2.15, in this same courtroom, I think. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
